subject: Creativity
title: How Real People Talk: Dialogue Isn't Speech
description: Learn How Real People Talk: Dialogue Isn't Speech in one minute.

hook.text: Record a real conversation and transcribe it. It's full of 'um,' repetitions, and dead ends.

buildup.text: Good dialogue SOUNDS natural but ISN'T. It's carefully crafted to feel real while doing work that real speech never.

discovery.text: Every line of dialogue must do at least one of three things: reveal character, advance plot, or create tension.

twist.text: Elmore Leonard said: 'If it sounds like writing, I rewrite it.

climax.text: Aaron Sorkin's dialogue sounds rapid and natural but is meticulously rhythmic — it's closer to music than to speech.

punchline.text: Great dialogue isn't realistic speech. It's a better version of it.

quiz.question: What must every line of good dialogue do?
options: Reveal character, advance plot, or create tension

details.summary: Effective dialogue sounds natural but is not actually how people talk. Real speech is full of filler words, incomplete thoughts, and meandering. Good dialogue is compressed, purposeful, and carries subtext while maintaining the illusion of real conversation.
details.whyItMatters: Dialogue is one of the most challenging aspects of writing because it must simultaneously sound natural, reveal character, advance plot, and carry subtext. Transcribing actual speech produces unreadable text.
takeaways: Written dialogue distills real speech into purposeful exchange
Every line should serve character, plot, or theme
The illusion of realism matters more than actual realism

faq.question: How do you make dialogue sound natural?
faq.answer: Read every line aloud. If it sounds stilted or overly formal, revise. Use contractions, interruptions, and incomplete sentences sparingly. The key is to create the feeling of natural speech while removing the waste that real conversation contains.

faq.question: Should dialogue always be grammatically correct?
faq.answer: No. People rarely speak in perfect grammar. Characters should speak according to their background, education, and emotional state. A professor might use complete sentences while a teenager might use fragments. Rigidly correct dialogue sounds robotic.
